phase1.explanation:
You've spent four units building the inside of a workshop nobody's ever seen. Every object, every class hierarchy, every exception handler, every ArrayList and background worker — all of it has been talking to you through [[term:System.out.println]], a single line of text in a black terminal. That's a workshop with no front window.

[[key:Unit 5 builds the storefront]] — the glass window and the shelves where customers who've never seen your code can actually walk up, click a button, and use what you built. That's what a [[term:GUI]] (Graphical User Interface) is, and [[term:JavaFX]] is the toolkit we're using to build one.

Every JavaFX app has the same three pieces, and they map directly onto the storefront: the [[term:Stage]] is the building itself — one per running app, created for you before your code even runs. The [[term:Scene]] is whatever's currently arranged in the window — the furniture, the signage, everything a customer sees right now. And a [[term:Scene Graph]] is just the arrangement itself: a tree of nodes, where the root holds children, which can hold their own children — a display case inside a shelf inside the window.

To open the shop, you extend [[term:Application]] and override start(Stage primaryStage) — Java hands you the empty building and says "do something with it." You build your Scene, call primaryStage.setScene(scene), then primaryStage.show() — and the doors open. [[warn:you never call start() yourself]] — main() calls launch(args), and launch() is what constructs the Stage and calls start() for you. Skip launch() and nothing happens; there's no building to put a window in.

One more thing worth knowing before you touch a single control: JavaFX runs its own dedicated thread — the [[term:JavaFX Application Thread]] — and [[warn:every UI update has to happen on it]]. If you kick off a long background task (a file download, a big calculation), do the work off-thread and hand the result back with Platform.runLater() — touching the window directly from another thread is a recipe for a UI that freezes or corrupts mid-render.

[[fun:JavaFX replaced an older toolkit called Swing]], which is still around and still works, but hasn't seen active feature development in years — Swing built windows the old, heavyweight way; JavaFX is hardware-accelerated, supports CSS styling, and lets you design the storefront in a separate file (FXML) instead of hand-nailing every shelf in Java code. We'll get there in a few lessons.

phase2.explanation:
No broken code this time — this lesson is the floor plan, not a build. But two myths are worth clearing up before we start nailing shelves together.

"JavaFX is dead, Swing is the only real option" — [[warn:not true]]. JavaFX is still actively maintained by the OpenJFX project, and it's the recommended toolkit for new Java desktop UIs. It just isn't bundled inside the JDK anymore as of Java 11 — you add it as a separate dependency, the same way you'd add any library.

"JavaFX can only make simple toy windows" — also not true. [[key:JavaFX handles charts, embedded web views, media playback, 3D graphics, and full animation timelines]] — everything from this lesson's plain Label window to a genuinely polished, professional desktop app is the same toolkit, just more of it.

phase3.openingDialogue: JavaFX — modern GUI for modern apps! 🎨

mcq.question:
Which statement about JavaFX is TRUE?

A) JavaFX doesn't support CSS styling
B) All UI updates must happen on the JavaFX Application Thread
C) JavaFX applications don't use a main() method
D) JavaFX is older than Swing

Select the CORRECT statement.

phase5.trivia: Stage and Scene aren't Java-chan's naming choice — [[fun:JavaFX borrows its vocabulary straight from the theater]]. A Stage is the physical structure, a Scene is what's currently set up on it, and you can even swap Scenes on the same Stage the way a play changes sets without tearing down the building. The storefront metaphor and the theater metaphor are really pointing at the same idea: a fixed venue, changeable contents.
